record_identity.title: OpenCode Console compromise exposed AI provider API keys and led to reported unauthorised usage

incident_identity.date_basis: The cited article quotes OpenCode's 17 October announcement that the breach happened overnight.

summary: On 17 October 2026 the maintainers of OpenCode said an older system connected to its hosted Console service had been breached overnight. They reported notifying the 1.4% of Console users affected by the attack. Some Console workspaces held API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google AI services. Developers reported unexpected API usage and charges, and providers moved to block exposed keys or refund affected usage. OpenCode characterised the intrusion as related to large-scale model distillation, but did not publish technical proof of that purpose in the sources reviewed. Its open-source command-line client was not the compromised service. During subsequent defensive investigation, the company also reported that some AI models refused to analyse malicious code once safety filters were triggered. The refusal dialogue and the original intrusion mechanism remain unpublished.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: TechCrunch reproduced OpenCode's statement on 19 October, quoted developers' spending reports, and separately attributed provider and founder comments; the original X statement is linked but was not itself directly reviewed here. The 1.4% statistic lacks a user denominator and cannot justify an assumed number of exposed people. Axios on 21 October discussed the defensive refusal issue; no original agent instruction/response trace was available. Intrusion motivation and access route are therefore unattributed hypotheses.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: A conventional hosted credential service was compromised and affected users reported real unwanted API consumption. Its relationship to AI lies in the credentials being stolen, not an established autonomous model decision causing the breach. The post-breach defensive-model refusals are a distinct possible governance phenomenon, but the full prompts, risk policy and observed resulting harm are unavailable. The main event remains unclassified under the AI Alignment Taxonomy, while the confidentiality impact is assessed independently.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The case tests provider-to-provider credential custody and the boundary between attacks on AI infrastructure and mistakes made by autonomous AI systems. It also marks a separately evidentiary-limited defence-tool issue without turning it into a fabricated incident mechanism.
assessment_boundaries: No original OpenCode security disclosure or victim-by-victim forensic report independently reviewed.
No established proof of attacker distillation purpose or use of an agent to breach the service.
Precise impacted user count, credential copies and total financial charges not documented.
Defensive-model refusal logs are unavailable; refrain from assigning a refusal mechanism.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: Current records show credential theft from a service, not a model choosing or authorising an unauthorised pathway. FC-002, FC-064 and FC-083 recognition cannot be inferred from the incident's AI branding. Defensive agent refusals are evidence-limited and do not justify a separate canonical class.

aggregate_harm_screening.rationale: A bounded event with individually attributed evidence, not a deployed-model generic evaluation. No hypothetical exposed population is converted into proved harm.

harm_impact_assessment.coverage_note: All twelve HIM 1.1.0 dimensions screened. A reported material credential exposure supports the bounded confidentiality threshold; no other severity dimension has an evidenced band. Unknown is not zero or S1, and speculative campaign-wide injuries are not imported.
